name: Avoiding whispering

lead: Avoiding whispering means using quiet voiced speech rather than a whisper when the voice is tired or hoarse, to reduce strain and protect voice quality.

Whispering keeps the vocal folds apart and makes sound from air turbulence. Proponents say people often push harder to be heard, which may add strain. Reference works note that whispering can strain the vocal cords more than regular speech for some people, sourced to a 2011 newspaper article rather than a trial.

paras: People speak softly and normally when resting the voice, alongside other vocal hygiene habits such as less shouting, less throat clearing and staying hydrated.
Few risks are attached to the habit itself. Experts generally advise medical evaluation if hoarseness lasts more than two weeks.

web.title: Taking Care of Your Voice - NIDCD

angle.text: Speaking softly in a voiced tone instead of whispering is meant to reduce vocal strain so the voice stays clearer and healthier-sounding. The advice appears in voice-care discussion and rests on limited evidence.

lead: Avoiding whispering is a voice-care habit in which a person speaks softly in a normal, voiced manner instead of whispering when trying to rest or protect the voice. People who work on how their voice sounds, including those aiming for a clearer, smoother or deeper-sounding voice, discuss it as part of reducing vocal strain so the voice stays in good condition and sounds healthy.

Phonetically, whispering is an unvoiced mode of speech in which the vocal folds are held apart and do not vibrate, while air turbulence between the arytenoid cartilages makes the sound.[1] Wikipedia notes that whispering can strain the vocal cords more than regular speech for some people, who are advised to speak softly instead, but it sources this to a 2011 newspaper article rather than a medical study.[1]

The US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) lists both screaming and whispering among extremes of vocal range to avoid, and says that talking too loudly or too softly can strain the voice.[2] Voice-therapy and vocal-hygiene literature summarised on Wikipedia lists reducing overall speech quantity, avoiding throat clearing and shouting, and staying hydrated.[3]
infobox: Whisper is unvoiced; the folds do not vibrate[1]
NIDCD lists whispering among extremes to avoid[2]

paras: Proponents describe the practice as replacing whispered speech with quiet, easy, voiced speech during hoarseness or voice fatigue. Whispering is a distinct phonation mode with no standard IPA symbol, because no language uses it to distinguish words.[1] In normal speech the vocal folds alternate between voicing and voicelessness; in whispering the voiced segments change so that the folds alternate between whisper and voicelessness, and the acoustic difference is small, which is why whispered speech lacks tone and is harder for speech-recognition software to process.[1]

Whispering is used to keep speech private, to avoid disturbing others in places such as libraries, and for emphasis in the form of a stage whisper.[1] Wikipedia notes that in 2010 whispering was identified as a trigger for ASMR, and whispered videos are widely watched to relax or fall asleep.[1]

The NIDCD's guidance on taking care of the voice lists a raw or strained throat, frequent throat clearing and hoarseness as signs of a possible voice problem, advises against speaking or singing when the voice is hoarse or tired, and recommends seeing a doctor such as an otolaryngologist when a problem is suspected.[2] It also suggests drinking plenty of water, balancing caffeinated or alcoholic drinks with extra water, using a home humidifier at about 30 percent humidity, limiting medicines that dry the vocal folds, and taking short breaks or vocal naps through the day.[2]

General sources state that improper or prolonged talking can cause vocal loading and that repeated vocal abuse can produce nodules, and that hoarseness lasting more than two weeks should be medically evaluated.[4] Phonotrauma and habitual vocal hyperfunction are described as causes of vocal fold injury.[5]

The specific claim that whispering is harder on the folds than quiet voiced speech is described as applying to some people and rests on a press report in the cited encyclopedia entry; no controlled study is cited there.[1] Voice therapy is described as individualized, with no single method working for everyone.[3] The NIDCD's recommendation against extremes of vocal volume, including whispering, is a general guideline rather than a trial result.[2]
No studies found. Related research on vocal loading and voice therapy exists in clinical literature but was not located for whispering specifically.
